old: For that starting point, I use a provisional, author-developed bridge I call borrowed adulthood. It combines familiar practices—witnessing, modeling, supported action, and gradual transfer of responsibility—without claiming that the complete sequence has been validated as one treatment.
new: In my writing I will use my own, not yet validated word for this kind of bridge to start with: borrowed adulthood .

old: Witness, when needed. Notice what is present without demanding warmth, wisdom, or certainty. If you already distinguish the internal positions, move to the adult function you need.
new: - if need be, enable the child to get into a witnessing position (if you are experienced in distinguishing between your own positions, just skip this step and find out what kind of adult you need in the situation and access it)

old: Borrow one function. Choose a safe adult, mentor, older sibling, future self, spiritual figure, value, or written plan. Borrow only the warmth, boundary, or direction needed now.
new: Do you have an adult you can borrow from? If you can’t find one, you can always reach up and grab a little bit from a safe adult in your life, or from a mentor, or an older brother or sister, or from your future self, or from a spiritual figure, or from a value, or from a plan you’ve written out. Just borrow what you need.

old: Become the adult apprentice. Choose the exact words or action yourself and carry at least one small part.
new: Then, operating from this position of being an apprentice in the adult hat, do at least part of what you would want to do.

old: People assume inner-child work begins with the child. Very often, you meet the guard at the door first.
new: When you try to connect with your inner child, what do you expect to happen? Unless you’ve been doing this work for a while, you might expect that you’ll experience your inner child.

old: You sit down to connect and get numbness, cynicism, anger, sudden hunger, a phone urge, a sexual urge, planning, sleepiness, dissociation, or the thought, “This is stupid.” I wouldn’t call those failures. They’re often the protector making an appearance in its usual charming way.
new: But, what you’re more likely to experience is numbness, cynicism, anger, a strong desire to eat, check your phone, have sex, plan your day, go to sleep, dissociate or a voice in your head that says something like, “This is stupid.” It isn’t that you’re failing to connect with your inner child, it’s that you’ve run into your guard.

old: Rest also doesn’t require helplessness. Reduce decisions for a defined period, put unfinished tasks somewhere visible, and let the internal adult keep watch. You remain able to move, stop, and return.
new: Remember that even though you might be resting for a while, you still have options. You can choose to not make any decisions for a certain amount of time. You can put things on a list that are not completed, and hope that someday your adult self will pick them back up and finish them.

old: If the practice makes you more loving, grounded, relational, honest, and functional, continue gently. If it makes you more paranoid, sleepless, grandiose, isolated, frightened, or unreal, stop deepening and get support.
new: The General Rule is: if you find that what you're doing is making you more loving, more grounded, more relational, more honest, more functional, then it's probably OK to keep doing it gently. But if what you're doing is making you more Paranoid, sleepless, Grandiose, isolated, scared, or more and more unreal, then DON'T GO DEEPER! GET HELP!
